The Soviet assault on Tajbeg Palace in Kabul on the evening of 27 December 1979, which killed Afghan President Hafizullah Amin and opened the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.

Amin had taken power in September 1979 and had Nur Muhammad Taraki smothered, though he announced an illness. The Soviet leadership, led by Brezhnev with the defence minister, KGB chief and foreign minister, decided in December to act. They no longer trusted Amin, feared he might turn to the West, and believed he was driving the country into revolt.

Several hundred KGB and military special forces, including the "Muslim Battalion" of Soviet soldiers from Central Asia dressed in Afghan uniforms, stormed the hilltop palace in under an hour. Amin was killed. Soviet airborne divisions had already landed at Kabul airport and crossed the border.

Babrak Karmal, waiting in the Soviet Union, was named leader. Moscow said it had been invited in under a friendship treaty. Most of the world, including a large UN vote, called it an invasion, and the mujahideen fought on for ten years.
sum: The Soviet assault on Tajbeg Palace in Kabul on the evening of 27 December 1979, which killed Afghan President Hafizullah Amin and opened the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
